slices.label: Men outside the South
slices.source: 1790 census back-projected to late 1788, free adult men outside the Southern states; the 1790 census gives only free white males 16 and over, so men 21+ are estimated. Voters were men meeting each state's rules: most states required a freehold, property or taxpaying qualification. Electors were chosen by popular vote in 6 states; elsewhere (Connecticut, Georgia and South Carolina, whose legislatures chose, and New Jersey, whose governor and council chose; New York failed to appoint, and North Carolina and Rhode Island had not yet ratified) men cast no presidential vote. Free Black men could vote in some Northern states on the same or stricter terms.

slices.label: Women outside the South
slices.source: 1790 census back-projected to late 1788, women 21+ (estimated from age bands). No woman could vote for president this year: New Jersey's women with £50 of property could vote in state elections under its 1776 constitution, but its electors were named by the governor and council. Turnout is zero by law, not by estimate.

slices.label: White Southerners
slices.source: 1790 census back-projected to late 1788, white adults in Virginia, North Carolina, South Carolina and Georgia; only men meeting their state's property or taxpaying rules could vote (Virginia required a freehold). The South Carolina and Georgia legislatures chose their electors, so people there cast no presidential vote. North Carolina had not yet ratified the Constitution.

slices.label: Black Southerners, most of them enslaved
slices.source: 1790 census back-projected to late 1788, Black adults in Virginia, North Carolina, South Carolina and Georgia; the census gives free people of colour without age or sex before 1820, so adults are estimated. The great majority were enslaved and could not vote. Free Black men meeting the property tests could legally vote only in North Carolina (until its 1835 constitution); the other Southern states limited the vote to white men. In South Carolina and Georgia the legislature chose the electors, so no one there voted for president directly. North Carolina had not yet ratified the Constitution and took no part.

whatIfs.label: Everyone Votes
whatIfs.detail: Every adult can vote, and turns out.
whatIfs.assumption: Every adult votes. Non-citizens choose like naturalized citizens of their state and sex; Black Southerners like Black voters outside the South; everyone else as their group did in 1789.

runs.summary: Rerun with nothing changed, 1789 comes out as it did: Washington wins, 69–0. The closest state was Maryland, which went to Washington by 40.2 points. Every one of my 100 reruns reproduces it exactly.
howIGotThis: The numbers: the 1790 census counts carried back to 1789 and certified returns; every draw reproduces 1789 exactly before the change.
How sure: I reran it 100 times with different population and parameter draws.

women.name: Ruth Robinson
women.quote: I have no say in it, being a woman. My husband will vote, or he won't, but that's his affair to settle.
women.controlQuote: I have no say in it, being a woman. My husband will vote, or he won't, but that's his affair to settle.

men.name: Ernest Reed
men.quote: The General served us well in the war. A strong union means steady work at the mill and honest dealing with our creditors. That matters to men like me.
